summary:
Malaysia criminalises same-sex conduct and gender nonconformity under both federal and state law. Sections 377A and 377B of the federal Penal Code punish "carnal intercourse against the order of nature", covering oral and anal sex, for any person regardless of gender or whether the act is consensual and private; the maximum penalty is 20 years' imprisonment plus whipping. Sodomy was first criminalised in 1871. These provisions are not confined to Malaysian citizens and are used against foreign nationals.

Section 377D of the Penal Code adds a charge of "gross indecency", an undefined offence carrying up to two years, which remains a discretionary prosecutorial tool. Enforcement against consenting adults in private is uncommon and tourists are rarely targeted, but that discretion is not a legal protection and has been withdrawn at moments of political pressure.

Every one of the 13 states, together with the federal territories of Kuala Lumpur and Putrajaya, maintains Sharia enactments criminalising cross-dressing or "a man posing as a woman", alongside offences of liwat and musahaqah. Penalties reach three years' imprisonment, a fine of RM5,000 and six strokes of caning. These state offences apply only to Muslims; non-Muslim visitors fall under the federal Penal Code alone. State Islamic religious departments carry out enforcement, and the enactments contain no legal definition of transgender dress, so the line between compliant and offending presentation is set by officers on the ground.

Arbitrary arrest of transgender people is documented over decades, including repeated arrests of individual women more than twenty times, a mass arrest of 16 trans women at a wedding in June 2014, and a pattern of strip-searches and sexual assault by religious officials during detention. In July 2020 the Federal Territories Religious Affairs Minister announced that the Federal Territories Islamic Religious Department had his "full licence to carry out its enforcement actions" against transgender persons; the International Commission of Jurists demanded the order be revoked.

Violence against transgender women is lethal and largely unpunished. A trans woman was killed in Klang in June 2019, the third such killing of a trans woman in Malaysia in fewer than two months. Reporting on those killings is obstructed: investigators' working phrase, "the deceased can't speak for herself", reflects a process in which police mistreatment and impunity go unexamined.

Queue-free criminal exposure now extends to social venues. On 28 November 2025 police raided a male-only sauna in Chow Kit, Kuala Lumpur and arrested 208 men under section 377B, the largest such raid since 2022. Media were pre-tipped and detainees' faces and personal details were published; 17 civil servants identified among the arrestees were suspended from their posts. A magistrate rejected the police request to extend remand on the ground that no case had been made out under 377B, yet release was delayed and more than 130 detainees were still being held at one point, including 31 foreign nationals whose embassies intervened. Justice For Sisters mobilised bailors and legal aid. On 2 December 2025 the Home Minister said the provisions would be revisited; within days police raided another sauna in Penang. Earlier venue raids include a Kuala Lumpur gay bar in August 2018, a Halloween party with LGBTQ participants in 2022, and 11 shopping malls in May 2023 over the sale of Pride watches.

Identity documents remain controlled by the state. The Registration Department routinely rejects gender-marker changes, and a 1982 National Fatwa Committee edict holds that sex is determined at birth and is unaffected by reassignment surgery; the edict was never gazetted and is not legally binding, but it is applied in practice, including to invalidate marriages involving transgender people. In August 2016 the Kuala Lumpur High Court ordered the National Registration Department to update a trans man's identity card, reasoning that Article 5(1) of the Federal Constitution guarantees a right to live with dignity in one's gender; that judgment was overturned on appeal in 2017. The only successful documented marker change is historical: in 1975 the Registration Department recognised Sari Kartina binti Abdul Karim as female and the Johor Deputy Mufti permitted her to marry under Sharia law.

There is no explicit visa rule for transgender visitors. The nearest documented statement of entry policy is a 2001 declaration by then-Prime Minister Mahathir Mohamad that Malaysia would deport any visiting foreign cabinet minister or diplomat who is gay, and a warning to gay foreign ministers not to bring their partners. Same-sex marriage and any form of partner recognition are unavailable, and no political party pursues LGBTQ legal reform; Mahathir told the Cambridge Union in June 2019 that Malaysia cannot accept same-sex marriage.

Malaysian law provides no protection against discrimination or hate crimes on grounds of gender identity or sexual orientation. Custodial and institutional alternatives to prison are prescribed by the same Sharia enactments: sharia courts may commit women convicted of musahaqah to an approved home for up to six months, and may order cross-dressing and other offenders into counselling or rehabilitation in a religious institution for up to six months in some states, extended to a year by Terengganu's 2022 amendment.

Legal challenges have failed to remove the framework. The High Court denied a request to declare the Sharia prohibition on cross-dressing unconstitutional. The Federal Court struck down a Selangor cross-dressing provision in February 2021 and 16 Kelantan Sharia provisions in February 2024, but on federalism grounds about which legislature may enact the offence, not on the substance, and nothing under the federal Penal Code was decriminalised.
tangentialFactors:
Human Rights Watch's 2022 report "I Don't Want to Change Myself", based on interviews with 73 LGBT people across seven states between 2018 and 2021 plus journalists and lawyers, found state-backed discrimination permeating everyday life: censorship of LGBT media content and events, discriminatory denial of health care and employment, and arbitrary arrest.

Religious and political mobilisation has narrowed the space for reform. Reuters reported in August 2023 that Islamist opposition was foreclosing reform and deepening fear among LGBT Malaysians. Government-funded mukhayyam "rehabilitation" retreats had drawn 1,733 attendees by June 2021. In November 2024 Kelantan approved amendments to its entertainment law banning activities that promote LGBTQ behaviour.

A 2001 statement by then-Prime Minister Mahathir Mohamad that Malaysia would deport gay visiting foreign ministers or diplomats remains the clearest official articulation of how sexuality is treated at the border. Artist pressure has also drawn official response: in July 2023 the band The 1975 was forced to cut short its Good Vibes Festival set after Matty Healy criticised the country's anti-LGBTQ laws and kissed a bandmate.

Hate speech regulation covers sexual orientation but not gender identity: the Malaysian Communications and Multimedia Content Code 2022, section 6.1(ii), defines hate speech to include material that denigrates a person on grounds including sexual orientation, enforced through section 211 of the Communications and Multimedia Act. Since 1994 the government has barred anyone homosexual, bisexual or transsexual from state-controlled media.

Malaysia is listed by the Human Dignity Trust among jurisdictions that criminalise, with active litigation recorded alongside comparable cases elsewhere in Africa and the Indian Ocean. The United Nations Development Programme and the Asia Pacific Transgender Network have published a joint study of the country.
localsOnly:
State Sharia offences reach Muslim residents only, but for them the enforcement machinery is close at hand: state Islamic religious departments arrest, and sharia courts can impose imprisonment, caning and fines, or commit a person to an approved home or a religious rehabilitation institution for months at a time.

The 1982 National Fatwa Committee edict, though never gazetted and therefore not legally binding, is applied in practice. It bars Muslims from sex reassignment surgery unless intersex, holds that sex is fixed at birth, and underpins routine rejection of gender-marker changes by the Registration Department. The Registration Department recognised a transgender woman's female status once, in 1975; no comparable successful case has been documented since.

Conversion therapy is practised regularly in Malaysia and is openly promoted by politicians and religious leaders. Transgender residents report discriminatory denial of health care and employment alongside physical and sexual assault in custody, with prison terms served in male wards where sexual violence is documented.

The National Blood Centre of Malaysia prohibits homosexual and bisexual people from donating blood, in a policy that is gender-neutral in wording. Adoption is not restricted on orientation or gender-identity grounds: under the Adoption Act 1952 and the Registration of Adoption Act 1952 a single person may adopt regardless of sexual orientation or gender identity.
outOfScopeNotes:
Whether the Home Minister's 2 December 2025 statement that the section 377 provisions would be revisited has produced any legislative or charging-policy change is not established by the sources available here; the only sourced follow-up is a further police raid in Penang days later.

The sources do not state whether any current visa, arrival-card or immigration screening question asks about gender identity or transition status, or whether passport gender markers mismatching presentation trigger secondary screening. No explicit visa rule for transgender visitors is documented.

No youth-specific health-care access or medication-carrying finding for Malaysia appears in the sources reviewed; the entry on health care is general and adult.

The Human Dignity Trust profile lists active litigation in Malaysia without itemising the cases, their status or their likely timelines; the state of play beyond the February 2021 and February 2024 Federal Court decisions is unresolved here.

Whether the 1982 fatwa has since been gazetted is stated in one source as never having been gazetted, but no independent verification of its current administrative status is present in the inventory.
